page: The Vultr voc-s-2c-16gb-320s-amd is an Optimized Cloud Compute instance built on the x86_64 architecture. It provides 2 dedicated vCPUs from a single AMD EPYC physical core operating at a base clock of 2.0 GHz, supporting two threads per core. Memory capacity is configured at 16.0 GB of RAM, yielding an 8:1 memory-to-vCPU ratio (8.0 GB per vCPU). The instance includes 320 GB of local NVMe SSD storage and one complimentary public IPv4 address, operating without dedicated GPU hardware acceleration.

Benchmark results demonstrate strong single-thread performance alongside standard two-thread throughput constraints. The instance achieves top-tier results in stress-ng single-core tests (3423.78) and strong performance in Geekbench single-core (2100.0) and text processing (2542.0). Compression throughput is competitive, reaching 32.1 GB/sec in single-threaded gzip and 14.63 GB/sec in single-threaded bzip3 decompression. The CPU supports modern instruction sets including AVX-512, AVX512_VNNI, and AVX512_BF16. However, multi-core benchmarks show the limits of a dual-thread setup, with PassMark CPU score (5977.93) and Geekbench multi-core score (3757.0) falling into the bottom tier. Static web serving throughput is low at 2.28 GB/sec, and Redis SET operations execute at 5.47 million operations per second.

From an architectural standpoint, the instance balances a generous 16.0 GB memory pool and fast local NVMe storage against a lean dual-vCPU processing footprint. This makes it an efficient match for memory-sensitive, single-threaded services, lightweight relational or key-value caches, data ingestion workers, or small back-end application servers, while remaining constrained for highly parallel compute or intensive LLM inference.
description: The Vultr voc-s-2c-16gb-320s-amd is an Optimized Cloud Compute instance powered by an AMD EPYC x86_64 processor. It features 2 dedicated vCPUs derived from 1 physical core at 2.0 GHz, paired with 16.0 GB of RAM (8.0 GB per core) and 320 GB of local NVMe SSD storage. It operates without dedicated GPUs and includes one complimentary public IPv4 address. Benchmarks demonstrate top-tier single-core compute and solid compression throughput, bolstered by AVX-512 extensions. Conversely, multi-threaded throughput and memory-bound operations are naturally restricted by the low core count, resulting in modest PassMark multi-core and web serving scores. The platform is well suited for memory-intensive background utilities, single-threaded data processing, lightweight caching tiers, and localized application workloads requiring fast local storage.
